Managerial & Cost Accounting

Cost accounting, variance analysis, budgeting, transfer pricing, and internal decision support.

Lesson Lectures · learn

Every financial statement you've read so far was built for outsiders — investors, lenders, the IRS — and it answers exactly one question: what happened last quarter? Managerial and cost accounting is the photo-negative of that book. It's internal, forward-looking, unconstrained by GAAP, and it answers the only questions an operator actually loses sleep over: How many do I need to sell to stop losing money? What does this product really cost me? Did the overspend come from paying too much, or using too much? The single habit of this whole field is to stop sorting costs by what an accountant calls them and start sorting them by how they behave — fixed or variable, traceable or shared — because that's the only cut that lets you make a decision. This lesson builds that habit from a sub shop, an Airbnb, a cupcake bakery, and a movie theater's popcorn bucket. Hover the cards, scan the charts, and take the quizzes as you go.

1 · The founding split: managerial accounting answers a different question

Financial accounting reports to the outside world under strict rules. Managerial accounting serves the people inside the building, and it bends to whatever helps them decide. The corpus draws the line cleanly:

"Managerial or management accounting is the process of identifying, measuring, interpreting and communicating information to management to assist them in planning, decision-making and risk management… in financial accounting the target audience is external, and in managerial accounting it's internal."

— Accounting Stuff, "Financial vs Managerial Accounting" · in your corpus
Stop sorting costs by their name → sort them by their behavior: does this cost change when volume changes?

That one reclassification — fixed (doesn't move with volume: rent, insurance, salaries) versus variable (moves one-for-one with each unit: ingredients, shipping, card fees) — is the foundation everything else in this lesson stands on. A 10-K never shows it to you, because GAAP doesn't require it. But without it you can't compute a break-even, can't price a product, and can't tell a good overspend from a bad one.

2 · Contribution margin and the break-even point — the "sniff test"

Once costs are split into fixed and variable, the most useful number in business falls out almost for free: the contribution margin — price minus variable cost per unit — the slice of every sale that's left over to contribute toward fixed costs and, eventually, profit. The corpus teaches it with a $5 sub sandwich:

"We're going to subtract from the price these variable costs and that spread is something that we're going to call the contribution margin… $5 minus $3 is $2. So that spread is going to be contributed toward the remaining fixed costs."

— "Cost Volume Profit Analysis (CVP): calculating the Break Even Point" · in your corpus
Contribution margin = Price − Variable cost  ·  Break-even (units) = Fixed costs ÷ CM per unit

With $20,000 of fixed costs and a $2 contribution margin per sub, the sub shop must sell $20,000 ÷ $2 = 10,000 sandwiches just to reach zero. Below that line it bleeds; above it, each extra sub drops $2 straight toward profit. Click each band to see how revenue and total cost cross.

There's a second flavor for when you don't sell in neat units: divide fixed costs by the contribution-margin ratio (CM ÷ price) to get break-even in sales dollars. Here $2 ÷ $5 = 0.40, so $20,000 ÷ 0.40 = $50,000 in sales — the same break-even, expressed in revenue.

"CVP analysis I find to be so useful as a sniff test — is this a good idea or does this idea stink? That's what CVP analysis will help us to determine."

— "MA22 — Breakeven Point and CVP Analysis Explained" (the Airbnb case) · in your corpus

Treat the desired profit like an extra chunk of fixed cost you must cover: Units for target profit = (Fixed costs + Target profit) ÷ CM per unit. In the corpus's Airbnb case, a night rents for $150 with $50 of variable cost (CM = $100) and fixed costs of $2,000/month, so break-even is 2,000 ÷ 100 = 20 nights. If she wants $1,000 of monthly profit, she needs (2,000 + 1,000) ÷ 100 = 30 nights. The instructor's whole point: break-even isn't the goal — "she didn't do it to break even, she wanted to make a profit." Break-even is the floor; the target-profit version is the actual plan.

3 · Activity-based costing — when the "average" overhead rate lies

Direct materials and direct labor are easy: you can trace the eggs and the baker's hours straight to the cupcake. Overhead — the supervisor's salary, utilities, cleanup, the warehouse — is the hard part, because it's shared across everything. The traditional shortcut spreads it with a single blunt rate:

"We've estimated overhead to be a hundred thousand dollars… they're going to work about 10,000 direct labor hours this period. What is our overhead rate? Well, it's $10 per direct labor hour… this method works for a lot of companies, it's very simple, but everybody knows it's not perfect."

— "MA15 — Activity Based Costing Explained" (the cupcake bakery) · in your corpus

One rate works until two products consume overhead differently. A simple, low-volume product and a fiddly, support-heavy one can use identical labor hours yet impose wildly different real costs — and a single rate quietly subsidizes the expensive one. The tell, from the corpus: "selling more products but making less money… something smells funny here." Activity-based costing (ABC) fixes this by replacing one rate with several — one per activity, each with its own cost driver:

"An activity-based costing system says one overhead rate is not enough — we need several. We have so many different kinds of overhead… maybe direct labor hours isn't a good proxy; maybe it's the number of setups."

— "MA15 — Activity Based Costing Explained" · in your corpus

The full-length corpus example splits a factory's $1,000,000 of overhead into cost pools — assembly (driven by units produced), order processing (driven by number of orders), customer support (driven by support calls) — and charges each product only for the activities it actually triggers. Click each pool to see how the driver routes the money.

The cost: ABC "takes more information, it's actually more difficult to implement." You buy precision with effort — which is why it's a managerial tool, used only when the mispricing is worth the work.

4 · Standard costing and variance analysis — splitting "we overspent" into why

The last pillar is the operator's early-warning system. A standard cost is a pre-set benchmark — what an input should cost and how much you should use. The gap between standard and actual is a variance, and its sign tells you where to look:

"The difference between the standard cost and actual cost is known as a variance. If the actual cost is greater than the standard cost, management can likely anticipate a lower profit than expected."

— "What is Standard Costing? What is Variance?" · in your corpus

But a single "we spent $150 too much on popcorn" variance is nearly useless — because it lumps together two completely different problems. The whole power of variance analysis is splitting that total into a price variance (did we pay too much per unit?) and a quantity variance (did we use too much?):

"Is this because of the price — that we spent too much money on the popcorn? Or is it because of the quantity — that we used too much popcorn, putting too much into each bucket? … standard costing lets us parse that out."

— "Standard Costs and Variance Analysis" (the popcorn case) · in your corpus
Price variance = (AP − SP) × AQ  ·  Quantity variance = (AQ − SQ) × SP  ·  [A = actual, S = standard, P = price, Q = quantity]

Worked example — the movie-theater popcorn (real corpus numbers). Standards: 0.25 lb of popcorn per bucket at a $1.50/lb standard price. Actual month: you bought 800 lb for $2,200 (= $2.75/lb) and made 3,300 buckets, using all 800 lb. Build the three columns:

  • AQ × AP = 800 × $2.75 = $2,200 (what you actually spent)
  • AQ × SP = 800 × $1.50 = $1,200 (actual usage, but at the price you should have paid)
  • SQ × SP = (3,300 × 0.25) × $1.50 = 825 × $1.50 = $1,237.50 (what you should have used, at standard price)

Price variance = $2,200 − $1,200 = $1,000 Unfavorable — you paid $2.75 vs a $1.50 standard, $1.25/lb too much (a supplier or purchasing problem). Quantity variance = $1,200 − $1,237.50 = $37.50 Favorable — you used 800 lb when 825 were allowed for 3,300 buckets, so you were actually a touch thrifty with portions. The headline "$962.50 unfavorable" hid the truth: your popcorn isn't the problem — your supplier price is. One number became a specific, actionable diagnosis.

6 · Check yourself

A food truck has $9,000/month fixed costs, sells bowls at $12 with $4 variable cost. Its monthly break-even is:

CM = $12 − $4 = $8. Break-even = $9,000 ÷ $8 = 1,125 bowls. Each bowl contributes $8 toward fixed costs; it takes 1,125 of them to cover $9,000.

A company sells more units every year but earns less profit, and "something smells funny" in its costing. The likeliest fix is:

That's the exact ABC trigger from the corpus. A single rate misprices products that consume overhead unevenly; splitting overhead into activity pools with their own drivers reveals which product is really losing money.

Actual cost ran $1,000 over standard. The price variance is $1,000 U and the quantity variance is $37.50 F. What should the manager do?

The split is the whole point. A large unfavorable price variance with a favorable quantity variance says you paid too much per unit while using a bit less than allowed. The problem is procurement, not the line.

These numbers guide decisions — they don't tie to the income statement

The classic trap is treating managerial figures like GAAP truth. They aren't. Contribution margin isn't gross profit; a "standard cost" is a planning benchmark, not what you'll report; ABC allocations are useful fictions for decisions, not audited numbers. Two deeper cautions: (1) "favorable" ≠ "good." A favorable material-price variance can mean someone bought cheaper, lower-quality popcorn that then over-fills (or under-fills) buckets and wrecks the quantity variance — chase one and you create the other. (2) Break-even assumes the world holds still — constant price, constant variable cost, a clean fixed/variable split. The corpus is explicit that these are conservative "back-of-the-napkin" estimates, deliberately padded; treat the output as a sniff test, not a guarantee.

One subtlety → your bridge to the rest of the MBA

Notice the throughline: every tool here exists to answer a decision, and the right cost depends entirely on the question. Fixed-vs-variable powers pricing and operating leverage (your finance course will call the same split the driver of a firm's risk). Contribution margin is the hinge of pricing strategy — discount to fill empty capacity only if price still beats variable cost. ABC is really a question about unit economics and which customers to fire. And the deepest lesson — Goldratt's The Goal lurks here — is that "cost" is never one number: a sunk cost is irrelevant to tomorrow's choice, an allocated overhead can be a phantom, and the only cost that matters is the one that changes because of the decision in front of you. Learning to ask "which cost is relevant to this choice?" is the skill that outlives every formula above.

Your move

Pick one real thing you sell, run, or are thinking of starting (a side project, a service, even a bake sale). On paper: (1) split every cost into fixed (doesn't move with volume) and variable (per unit); (2) compute your contribution margin (price − variable) and your break-even (fixed ÷ CM) — then add a target profit on top and ask whether the required volume is realistic, the "sniff test"; (3) if you sell more than one thing, ask the ABC question: which product or customer secretly eats your overhead (orders, support, setups) that a single average rate is hiding? Then, next month, pick one input, set a standard for price and quantity, and at month-end split the variance — was your miss about price or usage? You'll find a decision you couldn't see from the income statement alone.

Accounting is like a large tree that has been there for years; it has many branches. There is Financial Accounting, Administrative Accounting, Tax Accounting, Auditing and simple Accounting Records. Generally, when people talk about accounting, they are referring to Financial Accounting. So what is financial accounting? We have a lot to explain, but I recommend watching this video to the end at least once to get an idea of ​​the whole concept. Let's begin! Imagine you are the owner of RUFF TIMES, a publication that specializes in covering the latest celebrity gossip. During March, you launch a promotion, an offer for annual subscriptions starting on April 1st. People go crazy for your stories and you end up selling $40,000 worth of new subscriptions, all in cash. The first step in financial accounting is to identify the transaction. Well, that's easy, I just told you, that you sold $40,000 worth of new subscriptions that start on April 1st and continue until March 31st of the following year.

So what do we do? It's time to make an entry in the journal, which is the record of a financial transaction, and it looks like this. You have a registration number, the date, a description of the transaction, the accounts affected, which in this case are Cash and Subscription Revenue, and you have the debit and credit for $40,000... Ruff Times is a serious business, so you're using the law of double-entry bookkeeping, which means that this transaction affects at least two accounts and the total debits equal the total credits. But why do we do it this way? What is the principle of double-entry bookkeeping?

The first thing you should know is that Financial Accounting is built on a very simple idea: What your business owns is equal to what your business owes. We call what your business has Assets, which are resources from which you can obtain a future benefit. Things like Cash and Inventory, but on the other side of this formula we use two different terms to describe what your business owes: Liabilities, when you owe it to third parties: creditors or suppliers and they represent obligations that you will have to cover in the future, and Equity, when your company Ruff Times owes you money (shareholder), owner's equity represents your share in the net assets of the business.

So Assets equal Liabilities plus Equity. This formula is called the ACCOUNTING EQUATION and has major implications. It was created a long time ago by this gentleman, in this book, and it revolutionized the way we record a company's transactions. It's the origin of double-entry bookkeeping, which states that there are two equal and opposite sides to every transaction because this accounting equation is always an equality that must be in balance. Debits and credits are the words we use to reflect these two sides. Credits represent the sources of resources, where the flows come from, while debits represent the destination of these resources.

Today, any company in the world uses double-entry bookkeeping, as does Ruff Times. In this case, you debit the Cash account for $40,000 to increase your Assets and credit Subscription Revenue for $40,000 to record your income. Still with me? I know it's a lot to take in, and these terms might not make much sense right now, that's okay, just give it some time and let it sink in. You can always go to my videos on accounting fundamentals and explore it all there. I mention it in more detail. I've included a link to that video below in the description, right below the red subscription button. I do n't know what that noise was, but it doesn't matter.

The next step is to transfer the journal entry to your General Ledger. The General Ledger is where you can accumulate all the financial information from a period's transactions. It contains the complete record of your accounts and journal entries. A long time ago, it was a huge book that you filled out by hand, but thankfully, we've progressed, and now businesses like yours use accounting software that compiles transactions in the General Ledger (like Korvi) as a central database. So how do we go from the Journal to the Ledger? You transfer it to your T-accounts. T-accounts are where you record, classify, and accumulate all transactions for a period.

Generally speaking, there are six groups of accounts: Assets, Liabilities, and Equity, which we know from the Accounting Equation. We also have Income and Expenses, and withdrawals, also called Dividends, which are included in equity as part of the equation. If you want to see how and why they are included there, you can watch my video about Capital. I've put a link in the description. The journal affects 2 accounts and we can represent this record by drawing two "T" accounts and naming them: Cash and Subscription Revenue. These are called T accounts and they help us visualize what is being recorded.

Charges go on the left and credits go on the right. When you recorded your daily sales, you debited $40,000 on the left side of your Cash account and credited $40,000 on the right side of your Subscription Revenue account as well. When we add up what's in each account, we have $48,000 in Cash (because there was $8,000 in that account before) and you have $75,000 in Subscription Revenue (adding the above as well). But Ruff Times has other accounts, a whole collection of Asset, Liability, Equity, Revenue and Expense accounts recorded in your General Ledger. You made your entry in March when you collected the cash from sales, but let's go to the end of your financial year on December 31st.

We need to do a Trial Balance before adjustments. What is a Trial Balance? It 's an internal report that summarizes the balances of all your general ledger accounts and helps us check for errors, but its true value lies in being the basis for preparing the Financial Statements, which we'll see soon. But what does a Trial Balance look like? Here's your ledger again, and from there let's move forward to the end of December. Creating a trial balance is actually quite simple; you put all your accounts and their ending balances in order, and that's it! The trial balance shows the final balance of all transactions that affect an account.

As always, charges go on the left and credits on the right. At the bottom of your Trial Balance you will have the total of debits and credits, which must be exactly equal because the accounting equation is always true: debits = credits. Verification is another way of saying test, which is what the Trial Balance is and was originally used as a test to check that your debits and credits were equal, or "balanced". This is a balance BEFORE adjustments because we haven't made any adjustments, but we will now because the financial year has actually ended, so we need to make some adjusting entries that recognize what are called ACCRUED transactions.

What is this? To understand this, you need to know the basic assumptions of financial reporting standards. Yes, accountants must be good at following rules, although the rules change a bit from country to country, but you can follow International Financial Reporting Standards or some variant of Generally Accepted Accounting Principles ( IFRS) or GAAP. These accounting regulations ensure that your financial statements accurately and reliably reflect the state of your business, which is very important because many people rely on financial statements to make decisions, particularly those who have lent you money or invested in your business.

In short, both systems of financial standards have one thing in common: they both require you to follow the accrual accounting method, which means you must recognize your revenue when you earn it and expenses when you incur them (even if you haven't paid them yet). This is how you should calculate your profit, but here we can see that Ruff Times didn't follow the rules in March when it ran its annual subscription promotion. These subscriptions started on April 1st, you collected the $40,000 in cash, and you recorded the total amount in the general journal on March 31st. This is called realized accounting and it is not the same as accrual-based accounting.

In realized accounting, you recognize income when you receive cash and record your expenses when you pay them. But receiving cash isn't the same as earning income. Let me show you. You receive $40,000 in cash in March, but you actually earned that income over the following twelve months, which is when you deliver your monthly Ruff Times publication. So, since today is December 31st, you've already recognized income for 12 months in this fiscal year, but you haven't yet "earned" the income for the three months you haven't delivered, and you'll "earn" it by the end of March of the following year.

But that's okay; that's what adjustments are for. Adjustments are journal entries made to bring the books into line with the accrual method. We can fix this situation by removing three of the twelve months of subscription income, which is $10,000 (40,000/12x3), and temporarily treating it as a liability, something like unearned revenue. This is a liability because we have it, but it's not yet income because we have to provide the service to our customers from January to March of next year. Let's take this to the general ledger and make an adjusted trial balance for this recognition. It's called adjusted because we've just made the adjusting entries.

We see that subscription income has decreased by $10,000 and liabilities have increased by $10,000. Your debits and credits are still in balance because there are two entries on opposite sides of the journal, the equality is maintained, and now you are following the rules because you are using the accrual basis of accounting. Well done! Now we can generate your financial statements, which are accounting reports that summarize your business activities over a period of time (ER) or as of a date (ESF). These are reports prepared for external users to give your investors, creditors, and banks a way to know the financial health of your business.

The 3 main financial statements are the Balance Sheet (Statement of Financial Position), the Income Statement, and the Statement of Cash Flows. We can build the 3 using your adjusted trial balance. Your balance sheet looks like this and gives us a snapshot of your business: assets, liabilities, and equity at a specific point in time, showing anyone who consults it your financial position. They can see what you have and what you owe at the end of a period. Now let's review the Income Statement. This summarizes the business's income and expenses over a period of time. It allows the user to analyze your financial performance from one period to another, and the generation of profits.

If the accounting were cash-based and not accrual-based, it would also show your cash flows, but we use the accrual-based method, so profit and cash flow are not the same thing. We keep a separate record of cash flow in another financial statement, the Statement of Cash Flows. This report summarizes the inflows and outflows of cash over a period of time. Once you have generated these 3 financial statements, you can send them to your investors, creditors, and banks. If Ruff Times were on the Stock Exchange, then investors around the world would be able to compare your performance against their expectations and decide whether to buy or sell shares of your business.

They will analyze your financial statements using financial ratios, something we haven't seen here yet. So if you want videos on those topics, let me know here in the comments. But we're not finished yet. Once you've prepared your financial statements, you need to make some closing adjustments to prepare your books for the following year. A closing entry is a journal entry made to close all temporary accounts such as income, expenses, and dividends. The Ruff Times journal would look like this: You must debit your income accounts and credit your expense accounts to close them and bring them to zero.

The profit of $26,440 goes to retained earnings within the equity section of the balance sheet. These are the profits you're setting aside for the future. So if we look at your ledger again, we can see that the income and expense accounts have been settled, and now you're ready to start the new year. Together, all these steps constitute the accounting cycle, and that is what accounting refers to. It is the process of identifying, recording, summarizing, and analyzing the financial transactions of your business and reporting them in financial statements. In financial accounting the target audience is external, and in managerial accounting its internal. Let me explain how that works. Both the Financial Accounting Standards Board, and the International Accounting Standards Board who respectively come up with US GAAP and IFRS, state that the primary users of financial statements are an entity's existing and potential investors, lenders and creditors.

That's because the main objective of financial accounting is to report on a business's financial health to these external parties. That's not say that other groups of people like Management, Regulators and the Public won't find financial statements useful. But keep it in mind that existing and potential investors, lenders and creditors are the main reason why financial statements exist. To protect these external parties that are funding or potentially going to fund the business. In contrast to this, in managerial accounting the target audience is all internal. The main objective here is to create internal reports to help the managers within the business plan for the future, make informed business decisions and manage risks which in turn will impact on performance and profitability.

Okay so now for difference number two. Outlook. When it comes down to it, Financial Accounting involves reporting on past transactions and events whereas managerial accounting is more focused on the future. Financial accountants put together reports like the income statement and the balance sheet to summarise transactions that happened over a period of time, or the closing balances of assets, liabilities and equity at a single point in time, in the past. This period of time, or point in time that we're talking about is always in the past. And its historical information that financial accountants rely on to build these financial statements.

On the contrary, management accountants make reports to help management make decisions that impact the future. Next up I'd like to talk about scope, because this is completely different for both of these accounting branches. In financial accounting the scope is broad. Financial statements consolidate the results of all of the different departments and business units so that external parties can get an understanding of the big picture of the whole business. Meanwhile in management accounting, the scope is much more narrow.

Management accountants like to slice a company up into different segments divisions and cost centres to provide the managers of all of these different areas with detailed reports to help them specifically. These reports might not be limited to financial information either. In financial accounting the focus is always on being objective and precise. Financial statements are meant to reflect a true and fair view of the business's state of affairs at the end of an accounting period.
